gloss: in fact; as a matter of fact
hint: formal; the facts are, contrary to belief
note: Fairly formal. Everyday speech usually says 其實 qí shí 'actually'. Compare 實際上 shí jì shàng 'in reality'.

example.pinyin: Shìshíshàng, tā zǎo jiù zhīdào le.
example.english: In fact, he knew long ago.

hint: mail, a message or a gift
note: In messages, 收到 shōu dào alone means 'got it / received'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ shōudào wǒ de xùnxí le ma?

note: Also used playfully: 你好討厭喔 nǐ hǎo tǎo yàn o! 'You're so annoying!' (teasing).
'To have a dream' is 做夢 zuò mèng; 夢到 mèng dào means 'to dream about'.

example.trad: 我昨天晚上做了一個很奇怪的夢。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān wǎnshang zuò le yī ge hěn qíguài de mèng.
example.english: I had a strange dream last night.

example.pinyin: Hǎo qíguài, tā zěnme hái méi lái?
example.english: That's weird, why isn't he here yet?

hint: interesting or amusing, not 'fun to do'
note: Common in everyday Taiwan speech (好有趣 hǎo yǒu qù). For activities that are fun, Taiwanese usually say 好玩 hǎo wán; 有意思 yǒu yì si sounds more mainland.

gloss: to be afraid of; to fear
hint: short everyday word, takes an object
note: Also 'to worry that': 我怕來不及 wǒ pà lái bu jí 'I'm afraid we won't make it'. Compare 害怕 hài pà 'scared'.

hint: a small group or a set
note: Also a measure word for sets and groups: 一組 yī zǔ 'one set / one group'. As a verb it means 'to form': 組隊 zǔ duì 'form a team'.

gloss: to pass by; to go through
note: As a noun it means 'what happened, the course of events': 事情的經過 shì qíng de jīng guò.

example.pinyin: Wǒ měi tiān dōu jīngguò zhè jiā diàn.
example.english: I pass this shop every day.

gloss: good-looking; nice; good (to watch or read)
hint: looks good; also a good show or book
note: For people and things: 你穿這樣很好看 nǐ chuān zhè yàng hěn hǎo kàn 'you look good in that'. For movies and books: 這部電影很好看 zhè bù diàn yǐng hěn hǎo kàn 'this movie is good'. The opposite is 難看 nán kàn 'ugly'.
Formal-sounding. In everyday speech 最後 zuì hòu is more common.

example.english: In the end he still gave up.

note: MOE reads the first syllable as jī; in 'how many' it is jǐ. Some speakers say jǐ hū.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jīhū měi tiān dōu hē kāfēi.
example.english: I drink coffee almost every day.

note: With numbers it means 'about': 大概十分鐘 dà gài shí fēn zhōng 'about ten minutes'. As a noun, 'the general idea'.

example.pinyin: Tā dàgài bù huì lái le.

note: Taiwan (MOE) reads the second syllable as shì; the mainland says yì shí. 意識到 yì shì dào means 'to realize'.

example.trad: 他突然意識到自己錯了。
example.pinyin: Tā túrán yìshì dào zìjǐ cuò le.
example.english: He suddenly realized he was wrong.

example.pinyin: Zhè fùjìn yǒu biànlì shāngdiàn ma?
example.english: Is there a convenience store around here?

note: 好玩嗎 hǎo wán ma? 'was it fun?'. 有趣 yǒu qù is 'interesting'. MOE also lists hào wán 'fond of play', which is rare.
Very common as 沒必要 méi bì yào 'there's no need'. Compare 必須 bì xū 'must'.

example.english: There's no need to go that far.

note: The first syllable is xìng (mood, interest). The other reading xīng means 'to rise, prosper', as in 興奮 xīng fèn 'excited'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ duì yīnyuè hěn yǒu xìngqù.

note: In casual speech people usually just say 對 duì 'right'.

example.english: Doing it this way is right.

note: 'To sing (songs)' is usually 唱歌 chàng gē.

example.english: He's still being treated in the hospital.

hint: formal; as opposed to in theory
note: Fairly formal. Everyday speech usually says 其實 qí shí 'actually'. Compare 事實上 shì shí shàng 'in fact'.

example.trad: 實際上，事情沒那麼簡單。
example.english: In reality, it's not that simple.
There are a lot of reporters outside.

hint: location, the front side; up ahead
note: 'In front (of)' and 'up ahead': 在前面 zài qián miàn. The opposite is 後面 hòu miàn 'behind'. Taiwan (MOE) keeps the full tone on 面 miàn.

example.english: The convenience store is just up ahead.

note: Casually, 'to be in jail' is 坐牢 zuò láo or 被關 bèi guān 'locked up'.

example.pinyin: Tā zài jiānyù lǐ dāi le sān nián.
example.english: He spent three years in prison.

hint: agreeing: 'it's true that…'; not què shí
note: The first syllable is dí, not the particle de; in 目的 mù dì 'purpose' it is dì.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn díquè hěn hǎochī.

note: 種 zhǒng means 'kind, type'; as 'to plant' it is zhòng. Casually 那 nà is often said nèi: nèi zhǒng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ bù xǐhuān nà zhǒng rén.
example.english: I don't like that kind of person.

note: MOE also lists shí zai with a light tone. As an adjective it means honest, down-to-earth: 他人很實在 tā rén hěn shí zài.

hint: right by the side of something
note: Goes after the thing: 我家旁邊 wǒ jiā páng biān 'next to my place'. 坐我旁邊 zuò wǒ páng biān 'sit next to me'.

Counts thin, flat things: 一片麵包 yī piàn miàn bāo 'a slice of bread', 一片葉子 yī piàn yè zi 'a leaf'. Also means 'film' in 影片 yǐng piàn. MOE also lists piān, used in a few colloquial words but rare in Taiwan.

example.pinyin: Wǒ chī le liǎng piàn miànbāo.
example.english: I ate two slices of bread.

note: Counts songs and poems: 一首歌 yī shǒu gē 'a song'. It also means 'head / first' in words like 首先 shǒu xiān 'first of all'.
Introduces what happens if the first part isn't done. In casual speech Taiwanese usually say 不然 bù rán instead.

example.pinyin: Yào chuān wàitào, fǒuzé huì gǎnmào.
example.english: Wear a jacket, or else you'll catch a cold.

note: A more formal word for 'still'. In everyday speech people usually say 還 hái or 還是 hái shì.
MOE also lists a reading lù, used only in a few place names; for the number it is always liù.

example.english: I get off work at six.

note: Some older speakers say qí before a 4th tone (七次 qī cì), but most Taiwanese keep qī.

example.pinyin: Yī ge xīngqí yǒu qī tiān.

note: A lucky number (from a Cantonese pun with 發 fā 'to prosper'; in Mandarin bā and fā don't sound alike). In chat, 88 means 'bye-bye'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ měi tiān zǎoshang bā diǎn qǐchuáng.
example.english: I get up at eight every morning.

note: Sounds like 久 jiǔ 'long-lasting', so it is a lucky number for love and long life.

example.english: I get off work at nine.

note: Builds the numbers up to 99: 十一 shí yī (11), 二十 èr shí (20). Listen for the tone: shí (ten) and sì (four) can sound alike in Taiwan accents.
Fills gaps inside numbers: 一百零五 yī bǎi líng wǔ (105). Also means small or scattered: 零錢 líng qián 'small change'. MOE lists a rare historical reading lián.

example.english: That's a hundred and five dollars in total.

hint: true to reality, not made up
note: Describes something that actually happened or is not fake: 真實的故事 zhēn shí de gù shi 'a true story'. Compare 真的 zhēn de 'really' and 真正 zhēn zhèng 'genuine'.
Usually with 離 lí: 離這裡很近 lí zhè lǐ hěn jìn 'close to here'. The opposite is 遠 yuǎn. 附近 fù jìn means 'nearby / the area around'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā lí gōngsī hěn jìn.
example.english: My home is close to the office.

note: Taiwan (MOE) keeps the full tone hòu miàn; the mainland often says hòu mian. The opposite is 前面 qián miàn 'in front'.
想像力 xiǎng xiàng lì is 'imagination'; 你想像一下 nǐ xiǎng xiàng yī xià 'just imagine'. (Taiwan and the mainland write it differently, but it sounds the same.)

example.pinyin: Hěn nán xiǎngxiàng tā huì zhèyàng.
example.english: It's hard to imagine he'd act like this.
